statement: How many four-digit numbers have at least two digits that are the same? For example, 1231 and 5559 count, but 1234 does not.

choices.misconception: I counted the four-digit numbers whose digits are all different and gave that count instead of the rest.
I counted the numbers with all digits different as 10 x 9 x 8 x 7 = 5040, letting the first digit be 0, and subtracted that from 9000.
I counted the numbers with all digits different as 9 x 8 x 7 x 6, forgetting that 0 can be used after the first digit.
I subtracted 4536 from 10,000, thinking there are 10,000 four-digit numbers instead of 9000.

hints: It is easier to count the numbers that do not count.
Complementary counting: find how many four-digit numbers have all four digits different, and subtract from the total number of four-digit numbers. Watch out for the digit 0 in the first place.
There are 9000 four-digit numbers. With all digits different, the first digit has 9 choices (not 0), then 9, 8 and 7 choices for the others.

solutions.reliable: Four-digit numbers run from 1000 to 9999, so there are 9000 of them. Count those with all four digits different: the first digit can be 1 to 9 (9 choices), the second any of the 9 digits not yet used (0 is now allowed), the third 8 choices and the fourth 7. That gives 9 x 9 x 8 x 7 = 4536. The rest have at least one repeated digit: 9000 - 4536 = 4464. The transferable idea: when "at least one" invites many cases, count the opposite and subtract.

whyOnTest: At least one questions invite messy casework; the test is seeing that the complement is a single clean product, then handling the zero correctly.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
